subject: physics

hook.text: Your soccer ball is just sitting in the grass. It won't move by itself — someone has to give it a nudge!

sandbox.prompt: Tap the ball to give it a kick. Watch what it does after.
caption_sequence: The ball sits still on the grass.
It rolls until it hits the fence.

text_by_grade.grade5: A resting ball stays resting. A rolling ball keeps rolling — until something like grass, a wall, or a foot stops it. That's called inertia.
text_by_grade.high: Newton's First Law: an object remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. On grass, friction is the net force that decelerates the ball.

prompt_by_grade.grade5: If nobody touches the ball, what does it do?

spontaneous_motion.message: Tricky part: things don't move on their own — that's a great thing to double check!

image_prompt: A soccer ball resting on grass, simple flat illustration, with a small motion-line question mark above it
image_alt: Illustration of a soccer ball sitting still on grass.

subject: physics

hook.text: Two friends kick the same ball — one soft, one strong. Which one sends it flying farther?

sandbox.prompt: Choose a kick strength and watch the ball zoom.
caption_sequence: Watch how far and fast the ball goes.
Bigger kicks send it farther, faster.

text_by_grade.grade5: A bigger push makes the ball speed up faster. A heavier ball is harder to speed up.
text_by_grade.high: Newton's Second Law: F_net = m·a. Example: a 0.45 kg ball kicked with 90 N accelerates at a = 90/0.45 = 200 m/s².

prompt_by_grade.grade5: Which kick makes the ball speed up the most?

push_size_confusion.message: Looks like the push-size idea got mixed up. Let's watch it side by side.

image_prompt: Two soccer balls mid-flight, one with a short motion trail (soft kick) and one with a long motion trail (big kick), flat illustration
image_alt: Illustration comparing a softly kicked ball with a short trail to a hard-kicked ball with a long trail.

subject: physics

hook.text: When your foot kicks the ball... does the ball do anything back to your foot?

sandbox.prompt: Kick the ball at different strengths and watch your foot too, not just the ball.
caption_sequence: Both push on each other at the same time.
The foot feels a push back.

text_by_grade.grade5: Every push gets a push back! Your foot pushes the ball forward, and the ball pushes your foot backward — same strength, opposite direction.
text_by_grade.high: Newton's Third Law: F(foot→ball) = −F(ball→foot), equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on different objects.

prompt_by_grade.grade5: When you kick the ball hard, what happens to your foot?

one_way_force_only.message: The push-back idea is the tricky part here — let's see it with arrows.

image_alt: Illustration of a foot and soccer ball with two equal arrows pointing away from each other, showing the push and push-back.

hook.text: Barbie's little car is parked. It won't roll anywhere until someone gives it a push!

sandbox.prompt: Tap to push Barbie's car and watch what it does.

text_by_grade.grade5: A parked car stays parked. A rolling car keeps rolling — until something stops it, like a curb. That's inertia.
text_by_grade.high: Newton's First Law applied to a toy-car system: constant velocity implies net force = 0; friction/curb contact provides the net force that changes its motion.

prompt_by_grade.grade5: Once Barbie's car is rolling, what keeps it going?

hook.text: Barbie wants her car to zoom fast. Should she push soft or push strong?

sandbox.prompt: Try different push strengths on Barbie's car.

text_by_grade.grade5: A stronger push makes the car speed up faster. A heavier car (more dolls inside) needs an even bigger push.
text_by_grade.high: F_net = m·a — for a fixed toy-car mass, acceleration scales directly with applied push force; adding mass (more dolls) requires proportionally more force for the same acceleration.

subject: physics

hook.text: Barbie jumps off her skateboard. What happens to the skateboard when she jumps?

sandbox.prompt: Try different jump strengths and watch the skateboard.
caption_sequence: The skateboard shoots backward as she jumps forward.

text_by_grade.grade5: When Barbie pushes off the skateboard, the skateboard pushes back on her — that's why it shoots away as she jumps!
text_by_grade.high: Newton's Third Law: F(Barbie→board) = −F(board→Barbie). Because the board has less mass, it accelerates more for the same force pair (this connects to F=ma, not unequal forces).

prompt_by_grade.grade5: Why does the skateboard shoot backward when Barbie jumps forward?

one_way_force_only.message: The push-back idea is the tricky part — let's see it with arrows.

hook.text: A ball sits motionless at midfield. Nothing changes its velocity unless a net external force acts on it.

sandbox.prompt: Adjust applied force and friction. Watch how the ball's velocity responds.
caption_sequence: Zero net force means constant velocity, including zero.

text_by_grade.high: Newton's First Law: an object remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. On grass, friction is the net force decelerating the ball; on a frictionless surface it would roll forever.

prompt_by_grade.high: A ball rolls at constant velocity on ice with negligible friction. What is the net force acting on it?

force_scales_with_speed.message: This suggests 'moving = force is acting' — a common inverse mix-up. Constant velocity means net force is zero, even while moving.

hook.text: When a foot strikes a ball, two forces exist simultaneously — one on the ball, one on the foot. Are they equal?

sandbox.prompt: Toggle force vectors on both foot and ball during contact.
caption_sequence: Both force vectors appear, equal length.

text_by_grade.high: Newton's Third Law: F(foot→ball) = −F(ball→foot). Equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, acting on different objects — which is why they don't cancel out.

prompt_by_grade.high: If the foot exerts 90 N on the ball, how much force does the ball exert on the foot?

options.label: 0 N, since the ball is light

unequal_force_pair.message: This points to the 'unequal force pair' misconception — a common one. The forces are always equal in magnitude regardless of mass; let's revisit why.

subject: physics

hook.text: A toy car + doll system rolls across a smooth floor at constant velocity. What does that tell us about the net force?

sandbox.prompt: Adjust surface friction and initial push. Observe velocity over time.
caption_sequence: Constant velocity means net force is zero.

text_by_grade.high: Newton's First Law: constant velocity (including v=0) implies net force = 0. Friction is the deceleration force on real surfaces; on an idealized frictionless floor the system's velocity is constant indefinitely.

prompt_by_grade.high: The car-doll system moves at constant 2 m/s across a smooth floor. What's the net force?

force_scales_with_speed.message: This suggests conflating 'moving' with 'force applied' — let's separate velocity from force with a free-body diagram.

image_alt: Free-body diagram of a toy car and doll with balanced forces summing to zero net force.

subject: physics

hook.text: The doll + car system has a combined mass of 0.3 kg. How much force is needed to accelerate it at 4 m/s²?

sandbox.prompt: Vary mass (add dolls) and force, observe acceleration change in real time.
caption_sequence: Doubling mass halves acceleration at constant force.

text_by_grade.high: Newton's Second Law: F = ma → F = 0.3 kg × 4 m/s² = 1.2 N. Doubling mass while holding force constant halves acceleration — an inverse relationship.

prompt_by_grade.high: If mass doubles and force stays the same, what happens to acceleration?

f_ma_inversion_error.message: This suggests a direct-vs-inverse relationship mix-up between mass and acceleration. Let's re-examine F = ma term by term.

image_prompt: A labeled diagram of a toy car and doll with mass and force vectors, showing an inverse relationship graph beside it
image_alt: Diagram of a toy car and doll with force and mass labeled, next to a graph showing acceleration decreasing as mass increases.

subject: physics

hook.text: The doll launches off a stationary cart. The cart recoils backward. What's the force relationship?

sandbox.prompt: Vary launch force and observe both doll and cart trajectories simultaneously.
caption_sequence: Equal-magnitude vectors appear on doll and cart.
The lighter cart accelerates more for the same force.

text_by_grade.high: Newton's Third Law: F(doll→cart) = −F(cart→doll), equal in magnitude, opposite in direction. The cart is lighter, so it accelerates more per F=ma even though the force on it equals the force on the doll — force pairs are equal, but resulting accelerations depend on each object's mass.

prompt_by_grade.high: The doll and cart experience equal and opposite forces, but the cart moves faster afterward. Why?

options.label: The cart has less mass, so it accelerates more for the same force
The cart experiences a bigger force
The doll experiences a bigger force

unequal_force_pair.message: This suggests conflating 'equal force' with 'equal acceleration' — a classic mix-up between the 2nd and 3rd laws. Let's connect F = ma with the force-pair diagram.

image_alt: Illustration of a doll launching off a cart with two equal opposing arrows and a smaller mass icon on the cart.
